a: The world will be written down for destruction
t: Written down, or thrown into the Pit?
p: The Ge'ez has the world written down for destruction; the Aramaic 4Q212, as Milik restores it, has the wicked works cast into the eternal Pit.

readings.plain: The world will be written down for destruction

readings.w: Aramaic 4Q212 (4QEnoch-g), column iv, first century BC, damaged; as restored by Milik (1976), p. 281
readings.en: they will be cast into the [eternal] Pit
readings.plain: They will be thrown into the eternal Pit

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez, the only complete text. The Aramaic is older, but the key word "eternal" is restored, so it is given as an alternative.

a: chosen righteous ones will be chosen
t: Chosen righteous ones, or witnesses of righteousness?
p: The Ethiopic texts differ slightly; the Aramaic 4Q212, as restored by Milik, says they are chosen as witnesses of righteousness.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez edition (1851), from the manuscripts he used
readings.plain: chosen righteous ones will be chosen

readings.w: Printed Ge'ez text of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
readings.plain: the chosen ones of righteousness will be chosen

readings.w: Aramaic 4Q212 (4QEnoch-g), first century BC, damaged; as restored by Milik (1976), pp. 280–281
readings.en: the chosen, for witnesses to righteousness
readings.plain: the chosen will be chosen as witnesses of righteousness

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez, the only complete witness. The Aramaic is older and may be closer to the original, but it is broken and partly restored, so it is given as an alternative rather than followed.
b: Milik thinks the Ethiopic "shortens" the phrase and loses the idea of the righteous as witnesses (p. 281). In his text the chosen are also given "sevenfold wisdom and knowledge" (p. 280), where the Ge'ez has teaching seven times over "about all his creation." In 4Q212 this line is followed directly by the text of 91:11–17, part of the evidence for the original order of the Ten Weeks (see the note at 91:11).

a: But you who have suffered, do not be afraid.
t: A sentence only in the EOTC text
p: The Ethiopian Church's printed text opens 96:3 with a sentence that repeats 97:4.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez edition (1851), from the manuscripts he used
readings.plain: But you who have suffered, do not be afraid.

readings.w: Printed Ge'ez text of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
readings.orig: ወአንትሙ ኢትከውኑ ከማሆሙ አላ ሰማዕተ ይከውን ዲቤክሙ ዝንቱ ከመ ሱቱፋነ ኮንክሙ ለኃጥኣን
readings.en: and you will not be like them, but this will be a witness against you, that you were companions of sinners
readings.plain: You will not be like them; this will be a witness against you, that you kept company with sinners. But you who have suffered, do not be afraid.

why: The added words are almost the same as 97:4 and do not fit here, where Enoch comforts the righteous. They were probably copied in by mistake from the next chapter.
b: In the EOTC text the sentence stands just before "and wail like sirens," which the Plain English Translation places at the end of 96:2, following the sense. So it is shown here at the start of 96:3.

p: Dillmann reads 'the lowly'; the EOTC text reads 'the sinners.'

why: The woes are about the rich crushing the poor, so "the lowly" fits; "sinners" is the most common word in these chapters and could easily replace a rarer one.

a: the prayer of the righteous will reach the Lord
t: The righteous, or the holy ones?
p: Dillmann reads 'the righteous'; the EOTC text reads 'the holy ones.'

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez edition (1851), from the manuscripts he used

readings.w: Printed Ge'ez text of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church

why: 97:3 has "the prayer of the righteous" with the same Ge'ez; Dillmann's reading keeps the two verses together. "Holy ones" might mean angels, which would change the sense.

why: The words are in every Ethiopic witness; only the verse break differs. The site keeps Charles's numbers so that 1 Enoch can be cited the way scholars cite it. The EOTC text ends with "and they will not delay" instead of "suddenly."

p: Dillmann begins in the third person, then switches to 'you'; the EOTC text uses 'you' throughout.

why: Dillmann's shift of person is the harder reading, and the Epistle shifts person often (97:1–2; 99:2). The EOTC text smooths it. The same difference comes back at 99:15.

p: In Dillmann the angels search out the deeds; in the EOTC text God asks the angels about them.

why: Both are good Ge'ez. Dillmann's reading fits 99:3, where the angels lay sins before the Most High; the EOTC reading fits 104:3. The Plain English Translation follows its base text.

a: Have hope, you who died in righteousness.
t: The day of your death, or you who died?
p: Dillmann reads 'hope for the day of your death in righteousness'; the EOTC text reads 'you who died in righteousness.'

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez edition (1851), from the manuscripts he used

why: Enoch is speaking to "the souls of the righteous," who have already died (102:5; 103:3–4), so "you who died" fits. The two Ge'ez words (ʾəllä, ʿəlätä) look and sound alike, so one could easily become the other.

a: "In those days," says the Lord, "they are to call the children of the earth and testify to them about their wisdom. Show it to them, for you are their guides, and rewards over all the earth.
t: Chapter 105: missing in the Greek, present in the Aramaic
p: The Greek papyrus goes straight from 104:13 to 106:1, but the Aramaic 4Q204, as Milik restores it, had chapter 105. This goes with the variant on 105:2.

a: beings on the earth who are not of spirit but of flesh
p: Both Ge'ez texts have unclear words here (ʾəllä yarbəḥ). The Aramaic, as Milik renders it, speaks of creatures of flesh, not spiritual beings.
